ai-at-work.title: Ansible positions automation as the trusted execution layer for agentic AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: Ansible, Red Hat Inc.’s automation platform, is emerging as the trusted execution layer that might bridge AI-generated insights and reliable IT operations, aiming to turn probabilistic agentic AI into
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Red Hat's Ansible is positioning itself as the safety net between what AI thinks it should do and what actually happens in your infrastructure, basically acting as a governor for AI-generated actions at scale. This matters because letting loose language models to execute commands directly sounds like a fun way to accidentally delete production databases at 2 a.m., so having a trusted execution layer that enforces governance is genuinely smart thinking. Finally, someone's admitting that AI agents need guardrails instead of just promising magic, which is refreshingly boring in the best possible way.

ai-at-work.title: Domain-specific AI is rewriting the rules of workforce management
ai-at-work.excerpt: The rise of agentic AI is reshaping what enterprise partnerships must deliver — and domain-specific AI is proving to be the real differentiator between systems that advise and systems that act. As AI
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Domain-specific AI is moving beyond generic chatbots to actually execute tasks in workforce management systems instead of just providing advice. This matters because your digital workplace stack's real value now depends on whether tools can meaningfully integrate with HCM platforms and take action, not just talk about it. The irony is that after years of "AI will transform everything," we're finally getting somewhere useful, but only if you pick partners who understand your actual business problems instead of just slapping neural networks on legacy systems.

ai-at-work.title: Redis debuts the much-needed memory layer for enterprise AI agents
ai-at-work.excerpt: Artificial intelligence agents have a memory problem and now Redis Inc., the database management startup, is trying to fix that with its new, real-time Context Engine. As the company explains, it’s al
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Redis launched a new Context Engine designed to give AI agents better memory capabilities so they can actually retain information and become useful enterprise workers instead of just chatbots that forget everything between conversations. This matters because digital workplace leaders are drowning in half-baked AI implementations that can't remember what they just did five minutes ago, making them more novelty than utility. If Redis actually delivers on this, it could finally turn those shiny AI agents gathering dust in your pilot programs into something that actually earns its compute budget, though I'll believe it when I see enterprises actually using it instead of just talking about it.
